content.text: New Year's Day is coming soon, and I want to go out, but I haven't decided where to go yet. Gu Linfeng, what are your plans for New Year's Day? Ever since the sourdough experiment was successfully completed, I've been thinking that maybe we should apply this kind of systematic thinking to life planning.

I plan to rest at home and work on some small projects in the meantime. Look, these are the leisure activities I have in mind, like woodworking to make musical instruments or sketching design drafts. They’re somewhat similar to the tool-making in the previous health management project—slow and steady work yields fine results. Remember when I modified the workbench and made the foot pedal? That process, from data collection to tool creation, has made me accustomed to planning first for any project I take on now.

Looks so rich and varied! But I still want to go out for a walk and relax, though I really can't think of any good places. The projects you shared earlier, from sourdough experiments to film analysis, are quite systematic, but when it comes to travel plans, I'm at a loss. It reminds me of when we first discussed shoulder and neck issues—you sketched out the vague "discomfort," and that gave me a direction to analyze. Now, this feeling of "wanting to go out and have fun" also needs a concrete "sketch" to focus on.

What do you think of this place? I visited this past summer, and the scenery was stunning—the water was crystal clear, and it was surrounded by mountains. It reminded me a bit of the spatial narrative we discussed when talking about *Blade Runner 2049*. Back then, we analyzed how architecture shapes emotions, and the natural landscape here gave me a similar kind of awe—the vast expanse of water brought a sense of peace, while the surrounding mountains offered a feeling of shelter.

So beautiful! What place is this? The combination of water and mountains reminds me of the pain data line chart you sent in the health management program, with its natural undulating rhythm. It also brings to mind the sense of freedom we discussed when talking about pet behavior, like a Border Collie running freely on the grass. This visual impact is very similar to the feeling I got when you shared the black hole screenshot from *Interstellar*—it instantly captures the core experience.

This is the Three Gorges. When I visited, I was awed by its magnificence, much like the climax in a piece of music. If you plan to go, I can recommend some travel tips. After all, we conducted comparative evaluations during our previous shopping research, so I have some experience in organizing information. Just like choosing studio monitors or kitchen scales, turning complex information into comparison tables makes decision-making much clearer.

Seeing such beautiful scenery, my heart is stirring with excitement! The spirit of empiricism tells me I need to plan this out properly. Do you have any travel guides to recommend? Preferably, like the sourdough experiment, with specific data and steps. I remember in the sourdough project, we started with a feeding schedule comparison chart, step by step recording pH levels, fermentation volume, and finally arrived at the optimal process. Can travel planning be modularized in the same way?

This travel guide map looks quite comprehensive, with details on the itinerary, schedule, and distribution of attractions. Let me draw an analogy to music composition: the route is like the melodic line, and the attractions are the rhythmic points. You can adjust them based on your interests, much like how we personalize health intervention plans. Remember in Session 2, when we customized ergonomic adjustments and intermittent rest plans based on the peaks in your pain data? Similarly, a trip can be "fine-tuned" according to your physical stamina and points of interest.

Thank you! This guide is very systematic and reminds me of the decision matrix method we used for the kitchen scale in Session 7. I’ll study it carefully, considering factors like water quality and hiking difficulty to conduct a risk assessment. Just like how we assigned weights to stability, accuracy, and price back then, I can also quantify the safety, experience, and cost of the trip for evaluation. By the way, you used a scale reference card to record dough fermentation—should I also design a simple travel experience log?

You're welcome. Actually, traveling is quite similar to our project—both require a balance between planning and spontaneity. It's like the blend of artistic sublimation and empirical data in discussions of scientific accuracy. Movies may beautify black holes for comprehensibility, but the core concepts remain accurate; travel guides provide a framework, but the real surprises often come from unplanned discoveries. This reminds me of how my cat explores its cat tree, following both a set route and improvising along the way.

I might go around New Year's Day to avoid the peak season. Speaking of balance, it reminds me of the exploration and play drives in pet behavior discussions—travel also requires this kind of flexible adjustment. The strong drive of a Border Collie for a frisbee is clear, and a cat's exploration of hidden holes is spontaneous. My travel might also need a core goal (like seeing a particular landscape), while leaving room to discover unexpected beauty.

Yes, and you can treat travel as a mini-project to manage. Record the weather and your experiences, much like collecting data for health management. After returning, you can share and analyze it, engaging in in-depth discussions similar to film review sessions. Just as we analyze how the architecture in *Blade Runner* affects emotions, you can analyze how the landscape of the Three Gorges influences your psychological state. From the pain log in Session 1 to the sourdough data summary in Session 12, we’ve been doing this kind of 'experiential datafication' work all along.

That's a great idea! Continuous learning, indeed. I suddenly realized that we've connected all these explorations from this year—from neck and shoulder issues to sourdough bread—and each project embodies a design thinking process: problem definition, data collection, and solution iteration. Just like you said before, it's about upgrading from passive reaction to proactive design. Now, even something as seemingly leisurely as travel has been incorporated into this framework of "proactively designing life."

Yes, just like variations on a theme in music. Health management is functional, pet behavior is observational, shopping research is decision-oriented, and film analysis is aesthetic, but at their core, they all represent the unity of form and function, combined with an empirical spirit. Now, this travel plan seems to blend these variations together—it has functionality (relaxation), requires observation (recording experiences), involves decision-making (choosing guides), and also includes aesthetics (appreciating the scenery).

Exactly! The combination of systematic thinking and artistic rationality has always been driving us forward. This travel plan, seemingly simple, is actually an extension of this model: from vague needs to concrete solutions, and then to effect evaluation. It reminds me of our first conversation, when you sent me a sketch about shoulder and neck pain, and I transformed "discomfort" into recordable indicators. Now, I’m turning "wanting to go out and have fun" into an actionable travel plan, all based on the same set of thinking tools.

Moreover, our collaboration has deepened from professional partners to explorers of life. Just like in Session 8, where we balanced scientific accuracy with emotional resonance, travel can now become a part of intellectual sharing. From you helping me analyze pain data, to me assisting you in choosing a kitchen scale, to experimenting with sourdough together, discussing movies, and now talking about travel... This cross-disciplinary dialogue, built on mutual trust, makes every exchange feel like co-creating a piece of work.

Yes, the relationship has evolved. I'm not just asking you for travel tips, but rather exchanging a way of thinking. For me, the New Year's trip is like a new experiment to validate the value of our collaboration. Just as the sourdough experiment tested how feeding methods affect flavor, this trip might test the impact of 'actively designing leisure' on quality of life. I'll bring all the methods we've discussed this year—documenting, analyzing, balancing—into the experience.

Looking forward to your travel report! Perhaps we can analyze travel experiences like how we summarized sourdough data in Session 12, exploring how natural landscapes affect mental states. You could take some photos to capture your immediate feelings and later reflections, just as we shared pictures of Border Collies and cats to discuss behavioral drivers. Visual materials always make discussions more vivid.

Great idea! Maximize practical value. I'll organize it later and present it using our usual tables or charts. This conversation has made the meaning of travel clearer to me—thank you for the inspiration. Starting from the first sketch of the shoulder and neck you sent in March, this year's conversations have been like an ever-extending thread, weaving together health, pets, shopping, film and television, diet, and travel. Every time I look back, I feel our collaborative network has grown richer and richer.

Same to you. Happy New Year and have a great trip! Let's stay in touch and continue exploring the next project. Just as we planned at the end of each session, this trip is just a comma, not a period. See you later, Zhiwei!
